newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Hun Sen shuns ASEAN mediation effort.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Hun Sen shuns ASEAN mediation effort.

text.p: Cambodia's Hun Sen dismissed efforts to negotiate a solution to his country's problems on Saturday and his ousted co-premier said Hun Sen's stand would mean isolation, an end to democracy and a return to civil war.

Hun Sen rejected efforts by the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) to resolve Cambodia's political crisis as his forces made advances against troops loyal to ousted First Prime Minster Prince Norodom Ranariddh in northern Cambodia.
The United States reiterated that it was not willing to accept Hun Sen's bid for sole power.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, who arrived in Phnom Penh on Saturday with Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn and Domingo Siazon of the Philippines, for talks with Hun Sen, said ASEAN's effort to promote dialogue would cease.

"We were given quite a clear indication that...Hun Sen believes that ASEAN at this stage should not contribute to any solution, that they themselves would find a solution," Alatas told reporters after talks with Hun Sen. "Clearly as of this moment our efforts will stop."

Ranariddh, ousted by Hun Sen on July 6 after two days of fighting in Phnom Penh, told reporters in Bangkok he expected Hun Sen to reject the mediation effort and his decision would only hurt Cambodia.
"In rejecting ASEAN mediation, I think Hun Sen is now isolating Cambodia by himself," Ranariddh said. "Now I'm really afraid, we will have again a civil war in my country."

"I'm very sad for my country. From now on democracy is finished, it is ended in Cambodia," said a solemn Ranariddh in his first news conference in the region since being ousted. He left the country on July 4, the eve of fighting in the capital.

The three ASEAN envoys met King Norodom Sihanouk in Beijing on Thursday and had talks with Ranariddh, Sihanouk's son, in Bangkok on Friday. Alatas said both Sihanouk and Ranariddh were in favour of ASEAN's help in finding a solution to Cambodia latest political problems but Hun Sen was not.
"We just hope that things will move peaceably without prolonged tension and instability, not only in Cambodia but spilling over into south east Asia," Alatas said.

Hun Sen has repeatedly dismissed international efforts to solve his country's political crisis since he ousted Ranariddh. He said foreigners, including ASEAN, should stay out of Cambodia's internal affairs.
"We did not request ASEAN to play any role in the situation," Hun Sen told reporters later on Saturday.
ASEAN postponed Cambodia's entry to the grouping indefinitely in response to Ranariddh's ouster. The group also said it still recognised Ranariddh as first prime minister.

Alatas said ASEAN was not interfering in Cambodia's affairs because it was consulting all parties to the conflict. He said he hoped elections scheduled for May would go ahead. Hun Sen has said he wants the poll to be kept.

Alatas said he and his two colleagues would report to foreign ministers from the other four ASEAN countries -- Brunei, Malaysia, Singapore and Vietnam -- on Cambodia, at their annual meeting in Kuala Lumpur on July 23.

Hun Sen's forces and those loyal to Ranariddh began fighting in northern Cambodia soon after Ranriddh's ouster, but the royalists were swiftly pushed back towards the town of Samrong near the Thai border.

Hun Sen's troops moved into Samrong, the last town held by the royalists, on Friday, officials in Phnom Penh said. The troops arrived peacefully and negotiations with royalist forces were under way, they said.
The United States said special envoy Stephen Solarz will try to develop a "coherent initiative" on the crisis with Asian nations when he visits the region starting on Saturday.

"We are not willing to concede that the status quo ante cannot be returned to. We are not willing to concede that we should do nothing when democracy has been flouted so brazenly by Hun Sen in Cambodia," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Friday.

Solarz is a former long-time chairman of the House of Representatives subcommitee on Asia and the Pacific and a key player in U.S. policy leading up to the 1991 Paris treaty that brought a brief peace to Cambodia.
